name: Agent-as-a-Judge
question: Does the work really meet the spec?
summary: The judge is itself an agent. It opens files, runs code, searches the workspace and reads the trajectory, then checks each requirement with evidence. The approach comes from the Agent-as-a-Judge paper (Zhuge et al., 2024) and its DevAI benchmark of 55 AI development tasks with 365 hierarchical requirements. There it agreed with human experts far more often than LLM-as-a-Judge, at a fraction of the cost of human review.
useCases: Long-horizon tasks that produce artifacts: codebases, reports, data pipelines
Requirements that can only be verified by running or inspecting something
Replacing costly expert review of complex deliverables

items.detail: a requirement counts only if its prerequisites pass
verdicts backed by a file, output or log

steps: Break the task into explicit, checkable requirements
Give the judge read-only tools in a sandbox: file reader, code runner, search
Require an evidence citation for every verdict
Spot-check verdicts against human review on a sample
pitfalls: Slower and more expensive than a single LLM call
The judge agent makes its own mistakes, so audit it
It needs isolation so it can’t change what it evaluates
remember: Don’t just read the work. Inspect it and run it.
caption: The judge gathers evidence with tools before ruling on each requirement.

for rid in REQS:                     # dict order = dependency order
score = sum(v["verdict"] == "pass" for v in verdict.values()) / len(REQS)

steps.title: Prepare a sandbox
steps.text: Mount the agent's work read-only with no network, so the judge can inspect and run it without changing it.

steps.title: Let the judge gather evidence
steps.text: The judge agent reads files and runs commands, then rules on R1 with a citation: exit code 0.

steps.title: Respect dependencies
steps.text: R2 fails because the output is CSV, not Parquet. R3 can't pass without R2, so it's marked blocked.

steps.title: Score with evidence
steps.text: 1 of 3 requirements met. Every verdict carries evidence a reviewer can check in seconds.

outputs.name: Agent judge, dependency-aware

practice.scenario: A data team asks a coding agent to build a sales pipeline. A judge agent then opens the repo, runs the pipeline on sample data and checks 12 requirements, such as “writes output to Parquet” and “drops rows with missing dates”. Each verdict cites the file or log line it relied on, so a reviewer can confirm it in seconds.

industries.use: Verify agent-built features by running them, not just reading the diff
Check generated pipelines produce the expected tables and columns
Audit long reports against a requirement checklist, with sources

practice.analogy: A building inspector who walks through the house, turns on the taps and tests the wiring, instead of reading the builder's report.

library.name: Inspect AI
library.what: Runs agents with bash and python tools inside Docker sandboxes, which is exactly what a judge agent needs.

practice.note: Framework-agnostic sketch: agent_loop stands for your tool-calling loop (Inspect AI, LangGraph, or a model SDK).

samples.code:
import subprocess

REQUIREMENTS = [
    "R1: `python pipeline.py` exits with code 0",
    "R2: output/sales.parquet exists and has a `region` column",
    "R3: rows with missing dates are dropped, not zero-filled",
]

TOOLS = {  # read-only, run inside a sandbox
    "read_file": lambda path: open(path).read()[:4000],
    "run": lambda cmd: subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True,
                                      text=True, timeout=120).stdout[-4000:],
}

def judge(requirement: str) -> dict:
    return agent_loop(
        system=("You are a strict reviewer. Use the tools to gather evidence, "
                'then reply JSON: {"verdict": "pass" | "fail", "evidence": "..."}'),
        task=requirement, tools=TOOLS, max_steps=8)

report = [judge(r) for r in REQUIREMENTS]
score = sum(r["verdict"] == "pass" for r in report) / len(report)
print(f"{score:.0%} of requirements met")

numericDrill.question: Requirements: R1 builds (pass), R2 tests run (pass), R3 depends on R2 and writes CSV (pass), R4 depends on R3 and plots (fail), R5 writes docs (fail). What is the requirement satisfaction rate, in %?
numericDrill.answer: 3 of 5 = 60%. With dependency-aware scoring, R3 counts because its prerequisite R2 passed; R4 fails on its own evidence.

interview.question: When would you choose Agent-as-a-Judge over LLM-as-a-Judge?
interview.answer: When correctness can only be confirmed by acting: running code, opening files, querying outputs. LLM-as-a-Judge reads text; an agent judge gathers evidence. It's worth the extra cost for long, artifact-producing tasks.

interview.question: How do you stop a judge agent from damaging what it evaluates?
interview.answer: Run it in a sandbox with read-only mounts and tools, no network or write credentials, and time limits, and require an evidence citation for every verdict.

mistakes.mistake: Giving the judge the same write tools as the agent
mistakes.fix: Read-only tools in an isolated sandbox
Require a file, output or log citation for each verdict

quiz.question: When is Agent-as-a-Judge the right choice?
options: Grading the tone of a chat reply
Verifying a generated codebase meets its spec
quiz.explanation: It suits work that has to be run or inspected to be verified.

quiz.question: What should a judge agent’s sandbox have? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Isolate the judge. Never give it production credentials.

quiz.question: The coding agent’s summary says every requirement is met. Why not trust it?
options: The agent may overstate, so verify with evidence
quiz.explanation: A self-report is not evidence. Checking the work is.

quiz.question: R1 fails. R2 depends on R1 and looks fine. What is the dependency-aware verdict for R2?
quiz.explanation: R2 cannot count while its prerequisite fails.

quiz.question: What counts as good evidence for a verdict? Select all that apply.
options: The file path and lines checked
quiz.explanation: Evidence is something a person can check for themselves.

quiz.question: What is the main downside of Agent-as-a-Judge compared with LLM-as-a-Judge?
options: It is slower and costs more per evaluation
quiz.explanation: Running and inspecting work takes more time and tokens.

quiz.question: There are 4 independent requirements: 3 verified, 1 failed. What is the score?
You want a public set of AI-development tasks with requirement lists to test your judge agent. Which fits?
quiz.explanation: DevAI came with the Agent-as-a-Judge paper: 55 tasks with 365 requirements.

quiz.question: Where is Agent-as-a-Judge useful? Select all that apply.
options: Research reports checked against a requirement list
quiz.explanation: Single-word labels do not need a judge that acts.

quiz.question: How do you make sure the judge agent itself is right?
options: Spot-check a sample of its verdicts against human review
quiz.explanation: Audit a sample of verdicts regularly.

quiz.question: A requirement says “drops rows with missing dates”. What should the judge agent do?
options: Run the pipeline on sample data with missing dates and inspect the output
quiz.explanation: Test the behaviour with an input that exercises the requirement.

quiz.question: The judge marks “every figure cites a source” as passed, with evidence “the report looks well sourced”. What do you do?
options: Reject the verdict: evidence must name specific figures and their citations
quiz.explanation: Evidence has to be specific enough that a reviewer can confirm it quickly.

quiz.question: The judge agent had write access and “fixed” a failing test before judging. What is the problem?
options: None: the code is better now
The verdict is invalid; judges must be read-only so they measure rather than change the work
It should have fixed more tests
quiz.explanation: A judge that edits the work is no longer judging it.

quiz.question: A judge agent takes 6 minutes and $0.40 per project, and you get 500 pull requests a day. What is a sensible strategy?
options: Judge every PR with the agent
Run cheap code checks on every PR and the judge agent on risky changes or a nightly sample
quiz.explanation: Layer your checks: cheap and broad first, expensive and deep where it matters.

quiz.question: The judge agent ran out of steps before finishing requirement R3. What verdict keeps the judge’s own timeout from being charged to the coding agent?
quiz.explanation: No evidence means no verdict. Do not count a timeout as a pass or a fail.

quiz.question: Requirement: “the checkout button is disabled when the cart is empty”. What is the best evidence?
options: Open the page in a headless browser with an empty cart and check the button’s state
quiz.explanation: Observe the real behaviour in a running app.

quiz.question: Judge verdicts disagree with people on 20% of “performance” requirements such as “should be fast”. What is the fix?
options: Make the requirement measurable, e.g. “runs in under 60 s on 1M rows”
quiz.explanation: Vague requirements give inconsistent verdicts. Make them testable.

quiz.question: A contract generator must include 9 mandatory clauses in a 40-page document. Which approach fits best?
options: A single yes/no from an LLM judge
A judge agent that searches the document and gives a verdict per clause with its location
quiz.explanation: A verdict per requirement, with a location as evidence, is quick for a person to verify.

quiz.question: Why should the judge agent’s sandbox have no network access?
options: To stop data leaking and outside content influencing verdicts, and to keep runs reproducible
quiz.explanation: Isolation protects sensitive data and keeps results repeatable.

quiz.question: What makes requirements easy for a judge to check? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Vague requirements cannot be verified by anyone, human or agent.
